newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK OFFICIAL ATTACKS CRITICAL U.S. REPORT.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK OFFICIAL ATTACKS CRITICAL U.S. REPORT.

text.p: A senior Slovakian official on Wednesday criticised a U.S. report on NATO expansion which took Bratislava to task over its human rights record.
Emil Kuchar, general director of the Foreign Ministry's political section, told the official TASR news agency that Slovakia was in fact well-prepared for membership of the western alliance.
TASR quoted him as saying the U.S. report was "very superficial..."

Slovakia objects to a reference in the report to Congress which said that in the field of respect for basic human rights "serious problems have been noted in some (countries), such as Albania and Slovakia..."
Western diplomats usually list these as Bratislava's official treatment of ethnic minorities, its restrictions on press freedom and perceived lack of tolerance for political opposition positions.

Kuchar said: "A dialogue consists not only of one side formulating its reservations. What is important is the degree to which the other side is willing to listen to our arguments and the results of such a discussion."
He said Slovakia was as well-prepared for NATO membership as other leading candidates such as the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary.
Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's nationalist-populist coalition government has declared membership in NATO and the European Union as its top foreign policy priorities.

NATO member states are to hold a summit in Madrid in July to nominate the first candidates for membership from post- communist countries. Diplomats have said Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are most likely to be named.
NATO has said that basic criteria for membership include sufficient development of democracy, respect for human rights and the transformation to an open market economy.

Soon after the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Slovakia was considered among the top contenders for early NATO entry, but in recent years the United States and the EU have repeatedly criticised Bratislava for lagging behind in the development of democratic principles.
Washington's reservations on Slovakia were repeated by John Kornblum,, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European and Canadian Affairs, during a lecture in Bratislava last week.
"In our analysis there are questions on Slovakia and it appears that Slovakia has fallen out of the mainstream, but we are still not stating preferences," Kornblum said.
"Diversity, openness and tolerance are the way to a prosperous society. But we are concerned that this message is not being heard loud enough (in Slovakia)," he added. 121544 GMT mar 97
